name: Domaine des Bosquets Gigondas Le Lieu Dit... 2022
text:
## Domaine des Bosquets Gigondas Le Lieu Dit 2022

**The story.** Domaine des Bosquets sits high in the forested hills of [Gigondas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigondas_AOC), below the jagged limestone peaks of the [Dentelles de Montmirail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dentelles_de_Montmirail) ([see the estate from above](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Domaine+des+Bosquets,+Gigondas,+France&t=k)). "Bosquets" means wooded groves ([grove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grove_%28nature%29)), a fitting name, since many of its vineyards are isolated clearings surrounded by forest. The site was first mentioned as a vineyard in 1376. The oldest buildings still standing were built in 1644 under Jean de Rivière, [Seigneur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seigneur) de Laval: a defensive tower, protective walls and a solid [Provençal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provence) farmhouse, built for a remote corner of France far from the authority of [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris). In 1674 the estate passed by inheritance to the Chauvet family, who owned it for generations ([European Cellars](https://www.europeancellars.com/producer/domaine-des-bosquets/)).

In the 19th century Eugène Raspail reorganised and terraced many of the vineyards. In 1961 Gabriel Meffre found the property for sale, in poor repair, and bought it, partly for love of his wife Juliette, a Chauvet descendant. The couple finished Raspail's terraces and replanted much of the [Grenache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenache) and [Syrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrah) using cuttings from their friends the Reynaud family of [Château Rayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Rayas). When Gabriel died in 1987, the estate passed to his daughter Sylvette and her sons Laurent and Julien Bréchet. Julien took charge around 2010 (sources differ on the exact year); he trained at Château de Pibarnon in [Bandol](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+de+Pibarnon,+La+Cadi%C3%A8re-d'Azur,+France&t=k) and with the consultant [Philippe Cambie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Philippe+Cambie&go=Go) at [Château de Vaudieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Ch%C3%A2teau+de+Vaudieu&go=Go) in Châteauneuf-du-Pape, and considers 2015 his first truly independent vintage ([European Cellars](https://www.europeancellars.com/producer/domaine-des-bosquets/)). Vinous's Josh Raynolds wrote that in 2016 Bosquets made "not only some of the best wines of the appellation but of the entire southern Rhône".

**The vineyards and winemaking.** Julien farms 26 hectares, mostly in Gigondas, with a few in neighbouring [Beaumes-de-Venise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaumes-de-Venise) and [Sablet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sablet), at 175 to 425 metres. He has mapped 14 different soils, from sand to gravels and clays, some rich in [chalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chalk), and bottles the best sites separately in small quantities, without robbing his main Gigondas of its best parts. The estate is certified [organic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_farming) and uses biodynamic practices, with [cover crops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_crop) between the rows. The vines average 50 years old, and the estate as a whole is planted to about 70% Grenache, 20% Syrah, 8% [Mourvèdre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourv%C3%A8dre) and 2% [Cinsault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinsaut). Harvest is by hand, fermentation uses only the vineyards' own [wild yeasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yeast_in_winemaking), up to 30% of the bunches go in whole, and the single-site wines age in neutral, used French oak ([European Cellars](https://www.europeancellars.com/producer/domaine-des-bosquets/)).

**The wine: Le Lieu Dit.** "Lieu-dit" is the French word for a small named spot on the map, and this is a single parcel of old-vine [Grenache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenache) right next to the cellars. It was first made as a separate wine in 2009. The site is sheltered, surrounded on three sides by forest and partly shaded on summer mornings, facing north and north-west, so it ripens late and yields very little, about 16 hectolitres per hectare. The soil is sand and fine gravel over limestone bedrock, and the vines are 60 years old or more. It is fermented with 30% whole bunches and wild yeasts, then aged for 18 months in neutral 600-litre French oak demi-muids. About 380 cases are made in an average year ([European Cellars, Lieu-Dit sheet](https://www.europeancellars.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/12/Bosquet-Lieu-Dit.pdf); [producer page](https://www.europeancellars.com/producer/domaine-des-bosquets/)). The importer's sheet gives the altitude as both 325 metres (in the text) and 210 metres (in the table), so treat the exact figure with care.

**The vintage.** [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/southern-rhone) describes 2022 in the southern Rhône as hot and dry, saved by refreshing rains in mid-August. The reds are powerful but with fresh acidity, and for the most part incredibly age-worthy, with the finest likely to drink best over the next decade. She adds that Gigondas was somewhat less successful than Châteauneuf this year, which makes a cool, late-ripening, north-facing site like Le Lieu Dit, which stays fresh in a hot year, especially valuable.

**What the critics say for 2022.** As listed on the importer's sheet ([European Cellars](https://www.europeancellars.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/12/Bosquet-Lieu-Dit.pdf)):
- **[Wine Advocate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wine_Advocate): 95 to 97** (from barrel).
- **[Wine Spectator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine_Spectator): 94.**
- **[James Suckling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Suckling): 94.**
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 96** (from your CellarTracker list). The highest community score of any wine in your cellar.

I couldn't open the critics' full notes for this vintage, so the descriptions here rest on the estate's own description: a fine, late-ripening, sandy-soil Grenache.

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is just four years old. Your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2028 to 2039, and Jancis Robinson expects the finest 2022s to be at their best over the next decade. So this is still a young wine. I'd keep it for at least two more years; if you open one sooner, decant it two hours ahead to soften its youthful tannins.

**Serving.** For a single-site Gigondas like this, I'd serve it at about 16°C, a little below room temperature, and [decant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decantation) it an hour or two ahead when young, mainly to let it open; older bottles just need to be poured off their sediment. A large Burgundy-style glass suits the perfume.

**Food.** Gigondas is classic with lamb and game. My picks: a roast leg of lamb with garlic and [herbes de Provence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbes_de_Provence), [venison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venison) or wild boar, duck breast with olives, or a mushroom [risotto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risotto). Hard cheeses like aged [Comté](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comt%C3%A9_cheese) work too. I'd avoid very spicy dishes and sweet sauces.

**Value and where to buy.** None of the three stores on this site lists Domaine des Bosquets at the moment. In the United States the wines are imported by [European Cellars](https://www.europeancellars.com/producer/domaine-des-bosquets/) and turn up with their retailers. In my view, single-site Gigondas of this quality is good value next to Châteauneuf.

**From the history books**
- **A Roman holiday town.** Gigondas takes its name from the Latin *Jocunditas*, meaning joy or pleasure. It was founded as a place of rest for veterans of the Roman Second Legion, and a carved head of [Bacchus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dionysus) found there suggests wine was already made ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigondas_AOC)).
- **1376 and 1644.** The Bosquets vineyard is first mentioned in 1376; the fortified farmhouse, tower and walls date from 1644; and the Chauvet family inherited in 1674. Julien Bréchet still keeps the original handwritten 17th-century documents establishing the domaine ([European Cellars](https://www.europeancellars.com/producer/domaine-des-bosquets/)).
- **The great frost and a new appellation.** Until World War II, much Gigondas went to strengthen thinner Burgundies. The bitter winter of 1956 killed the [olive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olive) trees, and vines took their place. In 1971 Gigondas left the [Côtes du Rhône](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B4tes_du_Rh%C3%B4ne_AOC) Villages and became an appellation in its own right ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigondas_AOC)).
- **Cuttings from Rayas.** When Gabriel and Juliette Meffre replanted Bosquets in the 1960s, they used Grenache and Syrah cuttings from [Château Rayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Rayas), the famous Châteauneuf estate ([European Cellars](https://www.europeancellars.com/producer/domaine-des-bosquets/)).

**Curious details**
- **A tower for storm windows.** The estate's tower may look like a castle, but the importer jokes that today it is a handy place to store extra storm windows, because the [mistral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mistral_%28wind%29) is hard on windows ([European Cellars](https://www.europeancellars.com/producer/domaine-des-bosquets/)).
- **Mountains stood on end.** The Dentelles de Montmirail, the jagged ridge above the estate ([see it from above](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Dentelles+de+Montmirail,+Gigondas,+France&t=k)), were made when flat layers of Jurassic limestone were folded until they stood almost upright, then eroded into sharp spikes. The highest peak, St-Amand, reaches 734 metres, and the range is a foothill of [Mont Ventoux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mont_Ventoux), the highest mountain in Provence ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dentelles_de_Montmirail)).
- **Gravity in the cellar.** The barrel room sits directly below the fermentation tanks, so the wine can be moved by gravity rather than pumps.
- **Twenty-three hectolitres.** Yields at Bosquets average just 23 hectolitres per hectare for the village Gigondas and as little as 15 for some single-site wines, against the 35 allowed even in Châteauneuf ([European Cellars](https://www.europeancellars.com/producer/domaine-des-bosquets/); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **White Gigondas, at last.** Gigondas was a red and rosé appellation until September 2022, when white wines were finally allowed ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigondas_AOC)).
